candidates.title: Verifier-Augmented LLM for Intent→Configuration Safety
candidates.research_question: Does integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM-driven intent→configuration loop reduce the rate of unsafe/validator-failing configurations compared to an LLM-only baseline under realistic topology and vendor-CLI mixtures?
hypotheses: H0: Verifier-augmentation does not change the proportion of configurations that fail deterministic validation vs LLM-only.
H1: Verifier-augmentation (generate→verify→repair loop) reduces validator-failure rate by ≥30% relative to LLM-only on the chosen task set.
candidates.proposed_design: Assemble a task set of 300 intent→target-state tasks across synthetic but realistic topologies and mixed vendor CLIs. Implement two pipelines: (A) LLM-only: single-pass prompt→config; (B) LLM+Verifier: LLM generates config, deterministic network verifier checks; on failure, request LLM repair with verifier feedback for up to two repair iterations. Use the same LLM model/version and fixed prompts/seeds. Record verifier pass/fail, number of model calls, and latency.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records: intent, generated config(s) per attempt, verifier result (pass/fail + failing assertions), model-call counts, repair attempts, final pass status, time stamps.
candidates.primary_outcome: Proportion of tasks with final verifier-pass within allowed repair budget (compare pipelines). Secondary: mean model calls per successful task, time-to-pass, and distribution of remaining unsafe failures.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute proportions with 95% Wilson CIs; compare pipelines via paired McNemar test on per-task pass/fail and paired Wilcoxon on model-call counts. Report effect size (risk difference) and failure-mode breakdown (verifier-assertion categories).
risks: Deterministic verifier may be incomplete (false negatives): underestimates residual unsafe behavior.
Repair loop may oscillate producing more model calls than budget permits.
Synthetic topology/CLI set may not fully capture production diversity (external validity risk).

candidates.title: Verification-Aware Confidence Score for Predicting Config Correctness
candidates.research_question: Can a combined score that fuses deterministic-verifier feedback and LLM-derived uncertainty better predict whether a generated network configuration is actually correct (verifier-pass) than LLM-only confidence metrics?
hypotheses: H0: A combined verifier+LLM uncertainty score does not improve prediction AUC of verifier-pass vs LLM-only confidence.
H1: The combined score yields a statistically significant higher AUC (≥0.08 increase) in predicting verifier-pass on held-out tasks compared to LLM confidence alone.
candidates.proposed_design: Generate N=1000 LLM-produced configurations from a diverse set of intents (mixed vendors/topologies). For each sample, record LLM internal uncertainty signals (token-level entropy, log-prob, top-k gap), and deterministic-verifier outputs (binary pass, assertion counts, specific failed assertions). Construct features from both sources and train a simple logistic or isotonic regressor (train/validation/test splits) to predict verifier-pass. Compare baseline predictor using only LLM uncertainty vs combined predictor using verifier-derived features available pre-repair (e.g., failed-assertion types) and uncertainty.
candidates.expected_data: Feature vectors per sample, ground-truth verifier-pass label, model-predicted probabilities, ROC curves, calibration plots, and AUC/precision-recall metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: AUC (ROC) for predicting verifier-pass on held-out test split; report ΔAUC between combined and LLM-only predictors with 95% CI via bootstrap.
candidates.analysis_outline: Train repeated cross-validation; compute mean AUCs and bootstrap CIs; test ΔAUC significance with DeLong or bootstrap; present calibration (Brier) and precision@k analyses; analyze feature importances and failure cases where verifier features dominated.
risks: Verifier outputs may be unavailable or costly for large-scale sampling, limiting dataset size.
LLM internal uncertainty signals may be poorly correlated with correctness for some prompt styles.
Overfitting to verifier-specific failure signatures may reduce generalization to other verifiers.

candidates.title: Adversarial Robustness Benchmark for LLM-Generated Network Configurations
candidates.research_question: Are LLM-based intent→configuration generators brittle to small, systematic adversarial perturbations of intent or context, and which perturbation classes most increase unsafe/validator-failing outputs?
hypotheses: H0: Small adversarial perturbations to intents do not increase the verifier-failure rate vs unperturbed intents.
H1: Specific perturbation classes (negation flips, constraint elisions, ambiguous phrasing) increase verifier-failure rate by ≥25% relative to baseline.
H2: Tool-augmented (RAG/verifier-feedback) pipelines are more robust (smaller increase) to the same perturbations than LLM-only pipelines.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a benchmark of 400 seed intents; apply a suite of automated perturbation operators (synonym substitution, negation insertion, clause deletion, constraint paraphrase) producing adversarial variants. Run baseline LLM-only and LLM+tool (retrieval/verifier) pipelines on seed and perturbed intents. Use deterministic verifier to label safety. Report adversarial success rate per operator and pipeline.
candidates.expected_data: Per-sample results: seed intent, perturbed intent(s) with operator tags, generated configs, verifier outcomes, per-operator adversarial-success statistics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Adversarial success rate (increase in verifier-failure proportion) per operator and pipeline; rank operators by impact and compute pipeline robustness score.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate per-operator Δfailure with 95% CIs; compare pipelines using paired tests over same seeds; analyze operator × pipeline interactions; present qualitative examples of high-impact perturbations and typical failure modes.
risks: Adversarial operators may produce unnatural inputs not representative of real operator errors.
Benchmark conclusions may depend on chosen LLM and prompt templates (prompt-sensitivity threat).
High model-call budget required for broad operator coverage (cost/time risk).

candidates.title: Cross-Vendor Generalization Evaluation for Intent→CLI Translation
candidates.research_question: To what extent do contemporary LLMs generalize zero-shot to unseen vendor CLIs for intent→configuration translation, and how much labeled fine-tuning data is required to achieve operationally acceptable accuracy?
hypotheses: H0: A single LLM zero-shot produces correct vendor-specific CLI configurations at the same rate for seen vs unseen vendors.

H1: Zero-shot accuracy on unseen vendor CLIs is substantially lower (≥20 percentage points) than on seen vendors; modest fine-tuning with ≤200 labeled examples per vendor reduces the gap by ≥50% of the difference.
H2: Few-shot prompting (≤8 examples) yields intermediate gains but underperforms small fine-tuning in sample-efficiency terms.
candidates.proposed_design: Create a dataset mapping 600 intents to correct vendor-specific CLI sequences for three vendors (A, B, C). Hold out one vendor as unseen for zero-shot evaluation. Evaluate: (1) zero-shot LLM on unseen vendor; (2) few-shot prompting (1–8 shots); (3) fine-tune (or continued instruction-tuning) with varying labeled sizes (50,100,200 examples). Use deterministic verifier to assess correctness. Report accuracy and sample-efficiency curves.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task correctness labels (verifier-pass), token-level diffs, accuracy curves vs fine-tune sample size, and failure examples showing vendor-specific idioms missed.
candidates.primary_outcome: Verifier-pass accuracy on the unseen vendor under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tune regimes; report sample-efficiency (accuracy vs labeled examples) and statistical comparisons.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare accuracies with exact binomial CIs; test differences with two-proportion z-tests or corrected McNemar where paired; plot learning curves; analyze common cross-vendor error classes (syntax vs semantics).
risks: Synthetic dataset may not capture full vendor CLI quirks or enterprise policies.
Fine-tuning may exceed allowed compute or policy constraints for some hosted models.
Imperfect verifier alignment across vendors may bias accuracy estimates.
